metaTitle: Contractor Red Flags Ontario Homeowners Should Know
metaDescription: Six warning signs that a home service contractor in Ontario may not be legitimate, from cash-only demands to refusing WSIB proof, and what to do instead.
h1: Contractor Red Flags: Warning Signs Every Ontario Homeowner Should Know
summary: Cash-only demands, no fixed address, high-pressure pitches, no written scope, and refusing WSIB proof are the six clearest signs to walk away.
intro: Most contractors in Ontario are honest tradespeople trying to run a decent business, but every year homeowners lose money to the small minority who are not. The good news is that the warning signs tend to repeat themselves. Learn to recognize them early and you can avoid most of the trouble before a single tool touches your property.

sections.heading: Cash-only demands, especially with a discount attached

blocks.text: A contractor who insists on cash and offers to knock money off the price if you pay that way is usually not doing you a favour. In many cases this is about avoiding a paper trail, whether that is for tax reasons or because the business is not properly registered. A legitimate operation is generally happy to take e-transfer, cheque, or card, and will give you a proper invoice no matter how you pay.
A cash discount is not free money. It is often a sign that the transaction is deliberately being kept off the books, and that leaves you with no paper trail if something goes wrong.

This does not mean every contractor who accepts cash is a problem. Small trades sometimes prefer it for simple jobs. The red flag is when cash is the only option offered and it comes bundled with pressure to skip a written invoice or receipt.

sections.heading: No fixed business address you can verify

blocks.text: Ask where the business is based. A contractor who cannot give you a real address, or who gives you one that turns out to be a residential property with no signage or business registration attached, is harder to track down later if a dispute arises. Vehicles with only a phone number and no company name, or a website with no physical location listed anywhere, deserve a second look.

items: Search the business name plus the word 'Ontario' to see if a corporate or master business licence registration comes up
Check whether the address matches what shows on their invoice or quote
Look for a landline or a consistent business number, not just a personal cell that changes

blocks.text: A driveway crew with a truck and a trailer is not automatically suspicious, plenty of legitimate small operators work exactly that way. The concern is when a contractor actively avoids answering where they are based, or the address they give does not check out at all.

Door-to-door pitches that push you to sign the same day, deals that are only good 'right now', and salespeople who discourage you from getting a second quote are classic pressure tactics. Reputable contractors expect homeowners to compare quotes and are not threatened by the idea. If a person on your doorstep is leaning on urgency rather than letting the work speak for itself, slow the conversation down.

items.title: Ask for the quote in writing
items.text: A verbal-only quote with a same-day expiry is a pressure tactic. A written quote can wait a few days for you to compare.

items.title: Say you need to think it over
items.text: Watch how the salesperson reacts. Genuine businesses accept this without escalating the pitch.

items.title: Check them against a directory
items.text: Look the company up on /winners or a review platform before committing to anything.

blocks.text: This pattern shows up a lot with storm damage roofing pitches, driveway sealing crews going door to door in summer, and furnace or HVAC 'inspection' visits that turn into a hard sell. The service itself may be legitimate, but the sales approach tells you a lot about how the rest of the relationship will go.

A quote that just says a dollar figure with no description of materials, dimensions, or what is included is not really a quote, it is a guess you are being asked to sign off on. Before any work starts you should have something in writing that spells out what is being done, what materials will be used, roughly when it will happen, and what the total price covers.

items: Specific materials and quantities, not just 'concrete' or 'lumber'
What is explicitly excluded, such as permit fees or disposal of old material
Payment schedule tied to milestones, not one lump sum up front
A start date and a reasonable estimate of duration

blocks.text: Without a written scope, disagreements about what was promised almost always favour whoever wrote the invoice, and that is rarely the homeowner. This is worth reading alongside /resources/how-to-check-reviews-and-references before you sign anything, since the two problems tend to travel together.

sections.heading: Refusing to provide WSIB or insurance proof

blocks.text: In Ontario, contractors and their workers doing construction work are generally required to carry WSIB coverage, and a legitimate business can produce a WSIB clearance certificate on request, usually within a day. This certificate confirms the business is registered and in good standing, and it matters to you directly, because if a worker is injured on your property and the contractor is not covered, you could end up exposed to liability.

Ask for a WSIB clearance certificate before work begins, not after. A contractor who is genuinely covered can pull this up in minutes. One who stalls, changes the subject, or says it is not necessary for a job this size is giving you real information.

General liability insurance is the second piece. Ask for proof of coverage and, for larger jobs, ask whether your home insurer wants to see it too. Some homeowner policies have clauses about work done on the property, so it is worth a quick call to your own insurance broker for bigger projects like a new deck, roof, or foundation repair.

sections.heading: Asking for full payment up front

blocks.text: A reasonable deposit to cover materials is normal, particularly for custom orders like cabinetry or specialty windows. Being asked to pay the entire job cost before any work starts is a different situation entirely. It removes your leverage completely, if the contractor disappears, does poor work, or simply never shows up, you have already handed over the money with nothing to withhold.

items: A modest deposit tied to material costs is reasonable
Payments should generally follow progress, not precede it
The final payment should come after you have inspected the finished work
Be wary of any contractor who cannot explain why they need it all up front

blocks.text: This single red flag causes more homeowner losses than almost any other, because once the money is gone, your options for recourse shrink dramatically. It is one of the reasons /why-awards-matter focuses on contractors with a track record, since an established business rarely needs your entire budget before lifting a shovel.

checklist: Get at least two written quotes before agreeing to anything
Confirm the business has a verifiable, fixed address
Ask for a current WSIB clearance certificate
Ask for proof of general liability insurance
Insist on a written scope of work with materials and timeline
Refuse cash-only payment structures with no invoice
Never pay the full amount before work begins
Walk away from any pitch demanding a same-day signature

faq.q: Is it always a scam if a contractor asks for cash?
faq.a: Not always. Some small operators genuinely prefer cash for simple jobs. The concern is when cash is the only option offered, especially paired with a discount for skipping an invoice, since that removes your paper trail entirely.

faq.q: How much of a deposit is reasonable before work starts?
faq.a: It depends on the job, but a deposit that roughly covers material costs is common practice. Being asked for the full contract price up front is not typical and removes your ability to withhold payment if something goes wrong.

faq.q: What exactly should a WSIB clearance certificate show?
faq.a: It confirms the business is registered with WSIB and its account is in good standing, which matters because it affects who is liable if a worker is injured while on your property. A legitimate contractor can usually provide one within a day of asking.

faq.q: Where can I check a contractor before hiring them?
faq.a: Look them up on Google Business Profile and HomeStars for reviews, check BBB for complaint history, and see whether they appear among vetted businesses on /winners. Our guide at /resources/how-to-check-reviews-and-references walks through the process step by step.
